paper_title: DLP Dynamic Layerwise Pruning in Large Language Models
caption_used: Comparison of per-output and per-layer perplexity at different sparsity rates using a logarithmic scale. Both pruning configurations maintain comparable perplexity below 10^1 for sparsity rates up to 50%, after which values begin to diverge. At 60% sparsity, the Per-Output configuration reaches approximately 15 while Per-Layer remains near 10^1. The most pronounced separation occurs at 70%, where Per-Output perplexity climbs to roughly 50 while Per-Layer reaches approximately 25. At 80% sparsity, both configurations approach 10^3, with Per-Output exhibiting marginally higher perplexity than Per-Layer at this extreme.

model_annotations.Bulgarian: The bar chart illustrates the comparison of perplexity values between two pruning configurations, labeled "Per-Output" and "Per-Layer," across varying sparsity rates. The horizontal axis represents the "Sparsity Rate" with categorical labels ranging from 10% to 80% in increments of 10%, arranged in ascending order. The vertical axis represents "Perplexity" on a logarithmic scale, spanning from 10^1 to 10^3, with labeled tick marks at these powers of ten and intermediate grid lines indicating equal logarithmic intervals. The chart features two distinct bar groups for each sparsity rate: a blue bar representing "Per-Output" and an orange bar representing "Per-Layer," positioned side-by-side for each category. The bars are arranged in ascending order of sparsity rate along the horizontal axis. The height of each bar corresponds to the perplexity value for that configuration at the specified sparsity rate, with the values increasing progressively from left to right. At lower sparsity rates, both configurations exhibit low perplexity values, with bars approximately equal in height. As the sparsity rate increases, the height of both bars increases, with the orange "Per-Layer" bars generally being slightly shorter than the blue "Per-Output" bars, except at the highest sparsity rate where the blue bar is marginally taller. The chart does not include any visual emphasis such as shading or bolding to highlight specific bars.
